"Could not verify" is not "safe to destroy"; only `ErrLeaseNotFound` proves a lease gone.
"Is it safe to stop now" is answered by what the deployment holds (`alloc.Quiescence`) and then by the compute barrier, which asks the machines (`billet-capacity`).
"No files" reads as day one and day one mints a replacement that drops the whole fleet while the plane looks healthy.

(any other answer, or none, is could-not-tell and refuses, because a stopped daemon still has its registration on disk), writes its ownership marker before the daemon can register, bounds every call with `timeout -k`, and cleanup removes the key files unconditionally, checking each removal's status, deletes the registration only under that marker, treats a delete that finds it already gone as gone, reports every failure and keeps the marker until both the registration and `mdm.xml` are gone, so a deploy runner's or a laptop's own registration survives `reach: none` and a registration that could not be deleted is not forgotten.

10: per-shape price (refused).
11 and below decided a pooled runner's trust from the assignment that caused it to launch, which GitHub may reassign; lowering the floor to make an old fleet connect is offering to be wrong.
12: trust and cache scope are properties of a pool (the floor).
13: the range itself and the node's release (`VersionNodeRelease`, reported).
14: `CommandInventory` for the compute barrier (`VersionComputeBarrier`, mirrored as `alloc.BarrierWireVersion`; an older host is named "too old to be asked" rather than asked, because asking burns its single command slot for the whole timeout).
15: `CommandUpgrade` (`VersionNodeUpgrade`, gated where it is sent).
16: the installed manifest digest (`VersionNodeDigest`, reported; a digest from a pairing below this is dropped, not refused).
17: the CodeBuild fleet ARN (`VersionCodeBuildFleet`, refused, because two nodes naming one fleet each advertise all of it).
18: the CodeBuild registration path and region (`VersionCodeBuildRegistrationPath`, reported, since it only decides where the sweep looks).
19: `POST /v1/nodes/{node}/withdraw` (`VersionNodeWithdrawal`, checked where emitted; an older plane answers a bare 404 and the node says the plane is too old to be told).
20: `POST /v1/nodes/{node}/leases/{lease}/cache` (`VersionCacheObservation`, reported; checked where emitted in `nodeclient.Client.RecordCacheObservation`, which returns success without sending below it, because what an older plane loses is one diagnostic column on `job_history` and nothing a job depends on).
21: the tier label on `TrustedRunnerGroupRequest` (`VersionTargetedRunnerGroup`; a plane serving several GitHub targets needs it to know which owner's runner group a node is asking about, so an untargeted request from an older node is answered on a one-target plane and refused naming the version on several, because two organizations can each have a group of that name and guessing would vouch for the wrong owner's policy; the client sends the field only on a wire at or above 21, since the plane's strict decoder would refuse it on an older negotiated wire).
22: `CommandResult.Draining` (`VersionNodeDraining`, checked where emitted in `nodeclient.execute`).
23: the tier's cache block and the cache authority (`VersionCacheAuthority`, #226): `TierSpec.Cache` carries the normalised `config.CacheSpec`, a completion's destroy carries `Command.CacheAuthority` (the plane's verdict on whether the job's writes may publish), `GET /v1/nodes/{node}/leases/{lease}/cache-authority` answers the Actions cache for a live lease the node holds (`forOwnLease`, never an ended one), `?kind=` selects a cache on the policy route, and the build caches' outcomes ride `CacheObservationRequest`.
24: `VersionJobUsage`, two diagnostics.
25: `VersionProcessUsage`, what a job measured by its process's own accounting reports (a tart VM): the `oom` group named unmeasured, and energy with the source `process` and no idle share.
28 grants against a ceiling of 4 with the headroom check outside the transaction.
29 mutations, each neutering one path, each shown to fail a test.
29 redaction mutations run; three pre-existing gaps found (`Chain`'s three renderers, and both provider clients' tests holding members that could not leak).
2: node-contributed capacity and site (refused; a v1 node reads as zero).
31 on-demand CodeBuild builds: 31 distinct host boot ids (2026-09-02); reserved fleets keep a marker written by one build readable by the next.
42,940 restarts on a bare 404 from `/access_tokens` after an App was uninstalled.
53 (`job_cache_identity`) adds the JobStarted identity (`job_owner`, `job_repository`, `job_workflow_ref`, `job_event`) to `pool_runners`, and the completion's own `job_id` and identity to `pending_completions`, so a restarted controller compares two independent records rather than rebuilding one from the other; `StartPoolRunner` and `BindPoolRunnerJob` fill an identity once and never replace it, and the completion upsert keeps it for a redelivery of the same message.
54 (`cache_blocks_by_kind`) rebuilds the kill switch as `cache_blocks(kind, scope_type, owner, repository, disabled_at)`, carrying every older row as `actions` and using `'*'` for every cache; `ListCacheBlocks` is a `ReadOps` query.
55 (`build_cache_observations`) adds `sticky_cache`, `git_cache`, `bazel_cache` and `go_cache` to `leases` and `job_history`, first observation kept by the statements, and `ListCacheOutcomes` windows the history on `assigned_at`.

A 404 from S3 is two different facts, and only `NoSuchKey` is absence.
A 700ms mutex stall against a 300ms TTL reproduced `TestACancellationInsideTheLongPollStillDrains`'s CI failure exactly, and only under the old heartbeat ordering (`Listener.heartbeatLock` is the seam).
A CA directory holding one of its two files is refused rather than repaired; minting a replacement is a new authority and every node certificate stops verifying at once.
A CA's subject must name this deployment (`parseCA` refuses another's) and its key must be its certificate's key.
A CGO_ENABLED=0 Go 1.26 binary that never called `signal.Notify` for SIGUSR1 survived two SIGUSR1s and exited 0 when it finished (macOS 26, 2026-09-30, a throwaway probe); the Go runtime's handler drops an unwanted `_SigNotify` signal (`runtime/signal_unix.go`, `sighandler`).
A COMMA INSIDE A FLOW-SEQUENCE `argv` IS AN ITEM SEPARATOR: `argv: [systemctl, show, billet-node.service, --property=LoadState,ActiveState,MainPID]` handed systemd `--property=LoadState` and two unit names, which answered `LoadState=not-found` three times and refused every fresh-machine dry run (measured 2026-09-11 on the fleet's guest); quote any argument that carries a comma, and assert the exact argv in the gate (`converge-guard-check.sh`'s E7 does).
A CodeBuild holder-gone reproduction found a restart re-adopting a running teardown as custody (refused on every tend) and a teardown outcome that lived only in the dead process's memory; both fixed, both in `internal/e2e/holdergone_test.go`.
A CodeBuild service role holding only `ssm:GetParameters` resolves the parameter; `ssm:GetParameter` was dropped from the grant.
A DNS name or shared address requires `--endpoint-failover-verified`, the operator's assertion it survives removal, carried by `billet_retirement_endpoint_failover_verified`; retirement itself moves no endpoint.
A FAILED ATTACH BACKS OFF (`casRetryAt`, `casAttachBackoff`, five minutes, in memory only): the attach clones under the site's one cache index lock, and when a failure was remembered by nothing every request of the build ran it again, so one failure became a stream of lock attempts that starved every other session's cache work on 2026-10-03, including the Docker image store a guest's runner waits on before it starts (#320).
A Firecracker job boots a golden image: an Ubuntu 24.04 rootfs with Docker, the Actions runner and a small agent that reads its registration from the metadata service.
A GitHub release asset redirects to a pre-signed `release-assets.githubusercontent.com` URL carrying a SAS signature and a JWT, and `http.Client` reports that URL in its `*url.Error`, not the one billet asked for.
A MALFORMED published status is deliberately not a hold, since the `done` path repairs it from the journal and holding would make the host that needs the repair the one nothing can route into it; a DANGLING status symlink is unreadable and not absent (`ReadStatus` reads `NoFollow`).
A Mac's configuration is converged by `macos_node`, as the node account, and a change is a drain.
A PLACE IS WON FOR ONE PURCHASE, NOT FOR A BACKLOG (#248): a successful escrow re-dates a waiting buyer to now (`admissionQueue.bought`, called from `refillEscrowUngated`), so waiting tiers take turns one purchase each and a large shape at the head still holds freed room until it fits.
A PostgreSQL controller under the packaged unit gets its DSN from a whole unit rendered from the packaged one plus `EnvironmentFile=-/etc/billet/server.env`, the file the host role renders, never from a drop-in: `local up` and the host transaction refuse a billet unit with an effective drop-in, and the promotion rehearsal measured that refusal on 2026-09-04 before it rendered the unit the way the role does.
A RECORD FROM BEFORE THE PROTOCOL IS EXACTLY THE FIVE MEMBERS: `token` or `preparing` without `id` is refused by the command's decoder and by the fallback reader alike, because adopting it would mint another id, erase the token and settle a window without a settlement (round 7).
A RESUME TAKES THE TRANSITION'S OWN EXCLUSION (`withRetiringIdentityAccess`), because from `stopped` on the status this host published refuses every ordinary writer including this run, and an advance that recognises another run's move or rewrite FLUSHES WHAT THAT RUN OWED before publishing the phase that certifies it (a rename is visible long before its parent's entry is durable).
A REVALIDATING READ RE-CHECKS THE SCHEMA UNDER THE POLICY THE HANDLE WAS ADMITTED WITH: a standby and the upgrade probe (`db.standby`) use `verifySchemaNotAhead`, every other unlocked handle the exact `verifySchemaIn`; `View` once applied the exact check to every unlocked handle, and the watermark check inside a standby's or probe's own open reads through `View`, so a stamped candidate over a ledger one migration behind was refused `ErrSchemaBehind` at its open before it could claim and migrate, and every PostgreSQL host upgrade carrying a migration rolled back at the probe (found by review with migration 50, the first migration since the watermark check; `TestAStandbyRevalidatesUnderItsOwnSchemaPolicy`, `TestThePostgresProbeReadsALedgerOneMigrationBehind`).
A RUNNING BACKUP IS AWAITED AND NEVER KILLED, under a timer and never the record's clock (`retireNow` is a seam a caller pins, and a wait measured against it never ends), and the one failure reconciled is the refusal the retirement itself caused (a start after `timer_stopped_at`, `Result=exit-code`, `ExecMainCode` CLD_EXITED and `ExecMainStatus` 6), cleared with `reset-failed` and re-observed.
A SUCCESSFUL ANSWER AFTER THE ACQUISITION NAMES THE GUARD ALREADY HELD (`billet_exclusion_a.id == billet_exclusion_id` whenever an id is saved), because the fact is what every later call sends as `--expect-id`, and an answer naming another id made the next inclusion refuse the unchanged, settled guard as replaced, outside the cleanup's window (round 13).
A TIER HOLDS THE LINE ONLY WHERE ROOM COULD REACH IT: `waits` is recorded only when `alloc.AdmissionView` says the tier could grow once current work ends, so a tier at its own cap, pinned to a host that is gone, or with a shape no live host fits waits without freezing the fleet.
A VM that refuses to start used to surface as a delivery timeout, so `Launch` waits for the VM to be running and quotes the host's own reason from the run log.
A `--candidate` is admitted only inside a `recovery-*` child of the root, opened relative to the root, hashed through its descriptor, and the name compared with the descriptor afterwards, so a file swapped under the hold is refused rather than recorded under another file's digest; `prepare --candidate` hashes it again after its `version` and `status` probes executed it and refuses when the digest moved, so the candidate judged is the candidate recorded, and a probe that did not run or answered another shape is could-not-tell rather than a candidate with no version to compare.
A `--from-backup` retry reuses the copy its first attempt kept when the manifests match.
A `Candidate` needs a `Filesystem` with type, UUID and a proven-clean flag; non-empty alone proves neither.
A `Setsid` child of a launch agent survives `bootout` of that agent and keeps running after the agent's process exits (macOS 26, `realscheduled_test.go`); this is what lets the node agent start the updater that boots it out.
A `Setsid` child survives its agent's bootout (measured, `realscheduled_test.go`).
A `TagSpecification` on `CreateImage` is authorised as a separate `ec2:CreateTags` check keyed on `ec2:CreateAction`, measured with `create-image --dry-run`.
A `WriterLease` lasts across quiesce, filesystem verification and the fenced pointer CAS; a capacity lease stays charged until compute is proved gone.
A `bootout` returns in zero seconds with the process still draining, the service in the domain as `state = SIGTERMed` with its pid; billet captures the pid first and waits for both the domain and the process.
A `cas` object is stored only under the digest of its bytes; an `ac` record is the job's claim, at most 1MiB; above 90% full a write answers 507, a miss to the client.
A `codebuild` node may not declare a `site`.
A `done` JOURNAL IS ANSWERED BEFORE ANY CONFIGURATION IS READ AND BEFORE ANY LEDGER IS OPENED (`retireDone`, `cmd/billet/serverretiredone.go`), because the host it describes has no identity at its configured path and, when it kept no node, no configuration: the identity comes from the archive the journal recorded and the ledger from its locator.
A `done` journal dispatches to the completed path without requiring `RetainedInvocation`, its captured resource identities, its recorded configuration pathname or the old archive-input boundary.
A `fleetOverride` on `StartBuild` makes CodeBuild ignore the project's VPC configuration, which is why the terraform module refuses VPC inputs beside an adopted `fleet_arn`.
A `go build` inside a long reasoning run recompiles the tree and is the most common way one of these dies mid-flight.
A `go/analysis` analyzer in `tools/lint` is next, wired into CI only if it measures about zero current violations, because an analyzer that arrives with a backlog is one people route around (`wsl_v5` measured 5882 findings on this tree and was rejected on that number alone; a linter that wants every test named after the function under test flagged about half the suite, because billet names tests for the invariant they assert).
A `kill` that did not finish (an error, or launchctl ending at -1) may have delivered, so its record stays; only a proved refusal (a positive exit with the process alive) clears it.
A `local-down` seal is cleared by the next successful `up`; an `operator` seal (from `billet drain` or `local recover`) is left alone and reported.
A `pg_dump` inside the transaction stays rejected for ADR-008's reason.
A `systemd_service: state=restarted` held one SSH session for the whole drain, which has no bound: on the reference deployment on 2026-09-30 the session closed 34 minutes in, the converge failed as unreachable and released its guard, and systemd finished the restart afterwards.
A `uint64(stat.Rdev)` in the firecracker backend is a redundant conversion on linux and a required one on darwin; it passed locally and failed CI, and three defects on one branch had that shape.
A bare "review this diff" wastes the round.
A bare `404 Not Found` on `/access_tokens` is an uninstalled App or a stale installation, and `explainGitHubAccess` says so after a failure without replacing the error.
A bare int of bytes is how a memory limit ends up 1024x wrong.
A binary carrying `{1..42, 44}` and a ledger holding the same both say 44, the fence passes, and a later binary applies 43 after 44 there and before 44 on a fresh deployment.
A binary recovery ends at the fresh-converge boundary; only `ordinary`, confirmed cancellation and an already-settled retained entry's fresh admission open ordinary work.
A binary replaced by hand reports nothing rather than inheriting provenance.
A bucket that did not exist was therefore indistinguishable from a cold cache: every job fetched cold, the cache path fails open by design, and `billet check`'s own bucket probe printed that the bucket answered.
A build cannot be tagged, so ownership is a dedicated project plus markers.
A bump also brings GitHub's new tests and new assumptions about Azure, each of which becomes a difference: that bump's `configure-environment.sh` runs `update-grub` under `bash -e` for ext4 root options GRUB passes on Azure, and the cloud root filesystem has no GRUB, so `prepare:grub-absent` installs a stand-in that answers the call and removes itself; its tests assert those options on `/proc/cmdline` and the root mount, which the build's container shows as the builder's, and that apt goes through GitHub's mirror list; each such test is marked `-Skip` by name through `skip_upstream_test`, which refuses unless exactly one test has that name, so a renamed test stops the build at its prepare.
A cache bearer lives exactly as long as the compute it belongs to.
A cache publishes only what the ref GitHub proves may write, and reads are the pool's (#226, ADR-013).
A cache writer lease is not a capacity lease.
A cache's authority is proved from GitHub's record of the run, never from what the job says (#226).
A cancelled command is not a returned one.
A candidate whose exit never arrives after SIGKILL returns `hostupgrade.ErrUnsafeToRestore`, and so does an output (the probe's or the usage question's) still held open once the candidate has gone, or one that could not be read to its end, because the open pipe proves a live descendant and the unread one proves nothing; those verdicts outrank what the candidate said or how it exited; `Run` cordons without restoring, since a rollback over a live process is the one outcome worse than a hung probe.
A capability found by type assertion is proved on the value the assembly builds (`TestTheAssembledProvisionerOffersTheOfflineMemberRetirement` and the `var _` assertion in `internal/wiring`), never on a fake.
A change touching `.tf` files also needs `make tf-fmt-check tf-validate tf-test tf-lint tf-scan` before pushing — those are deliberately outside `check` because they need terraform/tflint/trivy installed.
A change touching `.tf` files needs `make tf-fmt-check tf-validate tf-test tf-lint tf-scan` before pushing; those are outside `check` because they need terraform, tflint and trivy installed (`make tools` installs the pins).
A change under `docs/` needs `make docs`.
A check that signs with one does not vouch for the other, so `billet check`'s healthy report says which it tested.
A clean `-race` run is evidence, not proof: it sees only the interleavings that occurred.
A clean exit withdraws; silence still means nothing.
A cleanup obligation is owed to the compute, not the lease: losing the lease changes who owns the capacity, not whether the container runs.
A clone larger than its tier's `max_size` (`store.VolumeSizer`) is discarded and the job starts cold; if the discard fails the clone is kept and used.
A code that does not redeem is discarded only on 404 and retried round-robin otherwise (422 also means the endpoint was spammed; 429 says nothing about the code), because discarding on anything else was a kill switch that left the App created and its key unrecoverable.
A codebuild-only sited tier advertised 0 with `billet check` healthy (first live acceptance re-run).
A collection installed from a Git tag reports the version in that file, so the cut-release workflow rewrites it.
A commitment made to a remote service cannot be revoked by a local timer.
A completed rollout is taken ONCE: its generation must exceed this host's SETTLED mark (`settled-decision`, raised by `settleCommitted` in `finishHostUpgrade` when the journal reads committed, a required step whose failure is a non-zero exit rather than the lost diagnostic a provenance failure is, and by the on-target no-op, never by an attempt that rolled back, so a rolled-back standby is asked again while a host an operator moved by hand is not moved back every five minutes); the on-target no-op (`settleOnTarget`, under the host transaction lock so it cannot bless another updater's unproven candidate) raises `last-decision` too, exactly as `actOnResolved`'s does, so a delayed older decision cannot pass the fence.
A completion that names NO runner is a job cancelled before any runner took it (read in one controller's journal, 2026-09-22), and its request id is the launch identity of the runner launched for it, which GitHub may have given another job: when that runner is bound to a different job, or is busy with one not yet known (recovered after a restart, awaiting its delayed `JobStarted`), the completion is `detached` (`resolveActualJob`) and `handle` settles, records, tears down and acknowledges nothing on its lease, only marking the job finished; an idle launch runner is still retired by it.
A compute host behind a residential gateway shares that gateway's NAT table with everything else at the site.
A concurrent `images reap` computes the kernels surviving generations need from the generations that exist when it looks, and between `installKernel` and `ImportGeneration` nothing names the new file, so it unlinks it correctly and the pull publishes a generation naming a kernel that is gone.
A connector token is a bearer credential and travels in the environment, never argv.
A consumer ISP gateway whose uplink dropped intercepted DNS to 1.1.1.1 and answered `github.com` with its own LAN address; the untrusted bridge's dnsmasq cached it and served it after the uplink recovered, so every untrusted job failed `actions/checkout` against a host the guard correctly drops, until a `kill -HUP` cleared the cache (measured 2026-09-23, #194).
A container renders its members' types, never their values (`awscreds.Chain` recursed forever and depended on every member redacting).
A content-addressed cache asks again every `casPolicyAge` (30s) while in use, and every publication asks again immediately before `PublishCAS`.
A contribution is detected only for a backend that runs work on the host.
A control plane authenticates under two issuers (the runner-group policy client signs with `app_id`, the scale-set client with `client_id` when set), so the healthy report says which it tested (`TestAVerifiedAppDoesNotVouchForAClientIdItNeverUsed`).
A controller's retirement is one row the two controllers contend for, and a `done` row is never deleted.
A converge restarts services, so never drive one from a runner billet manages.
A copied state directory keeps the original's identity on purpose (its containers carry that label) and `state.LockDeployment` is what makes the copy collide.
A crash mid-phase abandons rather than guesses, because a snapshot consumes the clone (`Journal.Consumed`).
A credential is never declared lost while its bytes are in memory, so a failed check writes the PEM to a fresh `O_EXCL` file and reports where it landed.
A declaration has three answers: absent (`DeclaredRange` treats a zero minimum as "speaks exactly the one version named"), valid, and contradictory (a minimum above the maximum), and the third is refused before any of registration's side effects run.
A default that cannot run is off; only a cache a tier turns on explicitly (`explicitGuestCaches`, `intercept` included) is refused on another backend or on a node without `node.cache`, or every existing Firecracker node file without a cache listener would stop loading.
A deferred `BEGIN` takes its read snapshot at the first read and asks for the write lock later; once a second writer exists, anything committing in between leaves the first holding a snapshot SQLite cannot promote (`SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT`, error 517, which `busy_timeout` cannot rescue).
A defined type (`type Static awssig.Credentials`) inherits none of them.
A deletion is authorised only by bytes all accounted for: the one-PEM-block proof checks the block starts where the file does, carries no headers and is the expected type, because `pem.Decode` skips forward to the first BEGIN and discards a remainder; and `parsePair` checks the certificate signed itself, because one assembled around the real public key satisfied every other check.
A deliberate downgrade is `--allow-downgrade` on `rollout start` (persisted in `Policy.AllowDowngrade`) and `host-upgrade` (on the journal): `ledgerHost.Migrate` lowers the mark through `SetReleaseWatermark`, the one write allowed to move it backwards, on a maintenance handle after the snapshot that keeps the higher mark for a rollback; on an external ledger, where `migrated` is skipped and the maintenance open is a read-only probe, `ledgerHost.ProbeReady` lowers it through the operator handle first.
A deliberate stop exits 0, or `systemctl stop billet-node` marks the unit failed after every supported drain.
A delivered start requires an already-active unit; a delivered stop requires an already-inactive unit.
A deployment is four things and they are useless apart: the ledger, the deployment identity, the GitHub App private key and the node-wire authority.
A deployment is named by a 32-hex identity (`internal/deploymentid`, `deploymentid.Validate`) minted once per state directory and recorded in the ledger's binding.
A deployment that says nothing updates itself; `automatic: false` is the opt-out.
A deployment updates itself unless `release.automatic` is written `false`.
A different target while one is open is refused (`ErrOpen`).
A discard is storage, not compute, and never runs on the node's command path (#223).
A discarded error is a vacuous assertion waiting to happen.
A docker generation needs a non-default runner group and at least one exact workflow.
A drain is two barriers, and the second asks the machines.
A drain waits for compute, not for entries.
A dry run compares across a pending daemon-reload and refuses only billet-owned policy that disagrees or cannot be compared.
A dry run of the preparation is answered by the executable a converge would be answered by.
A durable file is not a file nothing else will delete.
A failed `lstat` or `readlink` is could-not-tell (`operation-mask-unreadable`), never absence.
A failed exchange is ambiguous; neither headroom nor a missing report means zero advertised capacity.
A failed fetch names the URL it was on, and after a redirect that URL is signed.
A failed ping is not the place for any of this: `file is not a database (26)` is positive evidence the ledger answered and is broken.
A failed restore leaves the ledger fenced with a journal.

A failure up to the rename leaves nothing; a failed directory sync leaves the file, because the entry may already be durable and the retry re-verifies.
A fake `env` in front of the real one, recording its argv, is what proves no launcher went back to `env NAME=value`.

A fake must return what it is told and judge nothing.
A fake proves the shape of a request, never the values a real service refuses.

A fallback is a new purchase decision authorised atomically against node and deployment ceilings before the request is sent.

A fresh reservation during cancellation is this run's cleanup obligation.
A gate in the middle of a `;` chain is not a gate.
A gate's fake answers from those files and never from a shape written by hand; a role-side parser is written against the complete object of every fixture, nullability per branch included (a migration's `unchanged` has a null `endpoint` only under `record: none` or `unread`, a `reported` a null `to` only beside `node_removed: true`).
A gate's verdict is its exit status, captured before anything filters the output.
A generated boot script or buildspec is executed under `/bin/sh` in a test, never pattern-matched: a script that fails to parse is an instance that starts, registers nothing and reports success.
A generation NEVER goes to the trash: `rbd rm` refuses a parent a clone still reads before it deletes anything, and the trash would refuse nothing.
A generation of zero means an operator is at the keyboard; a `--rollout` with no `--generation` is refused.
A generation record is written before the current pointer, so an interrupted commit leaves the prior pointer or a complete new one.
A golangci-lint setting (a `forbidigo` ban, a `depguard` rule) is cheapest.
A goroutine dump showed nothing in flight: `waitForHolding` was ticking `Tend` over an empty custody map, and the hour-old custody warning never fired.
A green `make check` is necessary, not sufficient.
A group with selected visibility and an empty repository list routes nothing and reports nothing (the scale set registers, capacity is advertised, the job queues forever), so `billet check` refuses it; it is easy to reach through a REST `PATCH` that sets visibility without re-sending repository ids.
A guest booted with a different kernel fails mid-job, so they are published together and the generation records which kernel proved it (`SetKernel`, `KernelFor`), under the same cluster lock reaping takes.
A guest boots, takes its registration and runs a container in about ten seconds.
A gzip reader is multistream by default and tar stops at the first end-of-archive marker; `Multistream(false)` plus a drained tail is what refuses a second `billet` member.
A half-restored directory would start a control plane that mints whatever is missing.
A hard 85% on a project at 79% fails every PR and is learned to be ignored.
A heartbeat pass's budget starts after it holds the mutex.
A holder whose executable cannot be read is skipped only on ESRCH, because skipping an unreadable one could leave another VM looking unique.
A host below `VersionComputeBarrier` is reported as unprovable; `billet nodes decommission` bounds the expected set and its `--force` records the exclusion as durably unproven.
A host is moved onto the authority exclusion by an installer, and only an installer.
A host mount point is named by `sessionPathID`, a hash of the bearer, because the mount table and `mount`'s argv are readable by every local process.
A host saying it holds compute beats a completed run and may block but never clear (`provenBy` is the single definition the report and the decommission read).
A host that has not started and a host that installed, failed and rolled itself back are identical in every field; the dispatch records the epoch it was sent against (`rollout_nodes.dispatch_epoch`) and a higher one on the old release is the rollback, while an unrecorded epoch concludes nothing.
A job added to `ci.yml` must be in `verify-all-checks`' needs and either KEPT or in one family with that family's gate; a new input to a family must be added to its rule in the same PR, or the classifier skips it.
A journal write that fails AFTER its rename answers the phase the journal now HOLDS, with its durability said to be unknown, rather than naming a phase no reader would find.
A key is exactly a type, its material and an optional comment on one line, and its identity is the MATERIAL: `ansible.posix.authorized_key` removes by material alone, ignoring the type and the comment, and replaces the options of a key it already holds (2.2.2's source), so a line with options (whose quoted strings defeat any tokenizer but the module's), a value spanning lines, one material with two states or under two types, two present entries for one material and the break-glass key beside an absent or present entry with its material are each refused before anything is written; so are a comment where a key should be, an `absent`-only inventory, and keys for `root` under any policy but `yes` or `prohibit-password` (the policy is normalised before it is compared and rendered).
A later attempt that finds the lock held under such a cookie removes it at once, whatever its age, because the nonce makes it nobody else's.
A later authorized holder need not equal the historical journal owner.
A later refusal from GitHub ends an earlier grant.
A launch a draining node refuses says so in that field, and the plane records it through `alloc.NodeDraining`, which sets `drained = 1` on the host's current registration (fenced on epoch and incarnation) while the host stays live for the destroys its running work needs; `ListPlaceableNodes` then skips it until its next registration clears the mark.
A launch failure destroys the VM, and the guest's log is a pathname in a filesystem the guest controls: a job dispatched the moment the runner registers can unlink it, leave a symlink to anything readable, and choose the bytes billet prints. billet quotes only tokens from a closed set its own launcher wrote (`command-missing`, `started`), validated against that set.
A launch failure destroys the VM, so naming `billet-runner.log` points at a machine that no longer exists, and quoting its head lets a job (dispatched the moment the runner registers) choose the bytes billet prints.
A launch resolves the alias first, so the log names the generation.
A launch still in flight is NOT progress.
A launchd-managed node ran a real Actions job to green and destroyed its guest.
A launched lease with no row is still launching; a row naming another tier, or a status the report does not know, is unknown.
A leaf may not outlive its authority, so once the CA has less than a leaf lifetime left every certificate it issues is quietly shorter than the last, renewals come round faster, and then every node expires on the day the authority does.
A lease that had compute and stopped heartbeating is quarantined, still charged to its host, and leaves only on proof: the node's destroy report, an inventory that omits it after the grace, or an operator's `leases release --force`.
A lease that must survive a stall is proved on the allocator's clock, never by sleeping past a wall-clock TTL against the real ticker: `TestRenewalOutlivesTheShutdownRelease` slept two 900ms TTLs and failed on a loaded CI runner (2026-10-02, the test taking 21s) because a pass whose SQLite write outran its TTL/3 budget renewed nothing.
A lease whose completion GitHub already delivered settles as `done`, not as a provisional failure.
A ledger without its identity is a fresh authority that cannot see the compute the old one launched; an identity without the CA cannot issue a certificate; a CA without the App key cannot get a token.

A lint failure is fixed at the cause; a suppression needs a reason and is the exception.
A linter only analyses the files it would compile. billet is developed on darwin and runs on linux, so `make lint` runs golangci-lint for the host and again with `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64` (CI's architecture, not this Mac's arm64: `syscall.Stat_t.Nlink` is uint16 on darwin, uint32 on linux/arm64 and uint64 on linux/amd64, so `uint64(st.Nlink)` is a required conversion on two of them and an unnecessary one CI refuses on the third, and a `//nolint:unconvert` that quiets amd64 is an unused directive `nolintlint` refuses on arm64; the one spelling that passes everywhere is a generic widening, `widen[T ~uint16 | ~uint32 | ~uint64](v T) uint64`, as `cmd/billet/convergeguard.go` does; measured 2026-09-09), and `make lint-custom` runs `billetlint` for darwin/arm64 and linux/amd64.

A probe on the development Mac is not evidence about the builder.
A probe's answer that overflowed the command's output bound is refused as not read whole (`errOutputOverflow`), never decoded as complete, since a valid object, padding past the bound and garbage would otherwise pass the trailing-bytes check on the prefix that was kept; an exit 0 beside any other run error (`exec.ErrWaitDelay` from a descendant holding the output open past `guardWaitDelay`, a pipe failure) is refused the same way, since what was kept is what arrived before the wait ended; and the status decoder refuses a repeated member at any depth (`jsonRepeatedMember`, walked with `UseNumber` so a number the walk cannot hold is not where it stops, a walk that fails being a refusal and a repeated empty name being repeated), as the record's reader does.
A process launchd restarts after one exits (a non-zero exit) is asked in its turn, up to `maxDrainRestarts` (3) per stop, beyond which the service is crashing rather than draining and the stop ends Unknown.
A process named right after the ask that is not the one sampled means the service was restarted around the request: which of the two received the SIGTERM cannot be told, so the stop ends Unknown and asks nothing more, naming the record to remove.
A process restart forgets the record, and the stale bound remains the fallback.
A process's lifetime energy is the job's only from a reading within three intervals of the end.

A recap is parsed from the recap rows alone, and the pass's status is captured under `pipefail`.
A recordless running node is pre-R only when its image is the managed binary's AND the managed binary answers "unknown command" to `prepare --dry-run` AND the installed configuration has a node endpoint; anything else is `unknown` `record`, never a migration over it.

A refusal fragment in that gate is from a message, never a task name: Ansible prints every task's name whether or not it fails, so a fragment shared with the name passed with the assertion neutered (measured).
A refused `QueryRowContext` answers with a `Row` from `refusalRows`, a database whose connector never connects, so a refusal costs no ledger connection (four `View`s refusing together deadlocked a four-connection pool when the refusal ran a statement on it, and a statement run inside the transaction would abort a PostgreSQL one); `TestARefusedRowBorrowsNoConnection` holds it.
A refused dispatch records its reason, and `rollout status --json` is the ledger's own account.
A regex over a joined argument string is not a parser for what ssh sees: shlex leaves a token's inner quotes in place (`-o 'StrictHostKeyChecking="no"'`) and ssh strips them, so the judgement (`judge-ssh-options.py`, its own file so a test can call its decoder) walks the tokens as Ansible normalises them (stripped, empties dropped), interprets `-o` only, refuses every other flag (getopt clusters like `-4o...` would otherwise slip past a prefix test), and reads the keyword as OpenSSH's `strdelim` does and the value as its `argv_split` does (the escape set is the source's, not a guess: quote and backslash in either quote mode, space outside quotes only, nothing else); the rule is to implement the part of a grammar you can name, from the source, and refuse the rest, never to approximate the whole of it with a regex, and to assert the canonical refusal per spelling, because a parser that answers "cannot read" for every quoted form passes a table that only checks for a refusal.
A registration bumps the node's epoch; the process's incarnation is separate (a restart re-registers with a new epoch and the same process registers again after every control-plane restart), which is why `leases.holder_incarnation` records the incarnation of the process holding compute and never the epoch.
A registration discards the host's barrier run before the request is judged.
A registration epoch is the only causal evidence the coordinator has.
A registration proves who you are; only a command proves what you may do.
A related watcher introduced at the first boundary must leave the journal unpublished, configuration unchanged and phase unchanged; the temporary is left for inspection when the next step refuses.
A release asset caps at 2GiB, so `RootfsMultipart` carries up to `MaxParts` (64) parts of `MaxPartBytes`, assembled by `AssembleRootfs`; `Validate` refuses both-or-neither forms.
A release binary reported `0.9.1`, `version.Compare` accepted only `vX.Y.Z`, and every downgrade guard on a release was could-not-tell: a control plane moved to v0.9.1 by the Ansible role obeyed the morning's rollout to v0.9.0 six minutes later (`0.9.1 -> v0.9.0, reached committed`), because the role re-enables `billet-upgrade.timer` and a running rollout was never superseded when the channel moved past it (2026-09-05).
A release carries the binary, the collection and the module, so `billet_version`, `requirements.yml` and every `?ref=` should read one `vX.Y.Z`; cutting a release rewrites the READMEs from `main` to that tag.
A release is a semantic-version tag (`vX.Y.Z`, because Go resolves nothing else; staying on `v0` keeps the module path free of a suffix) cut from a `release/vX.Y` branch by the `cut-release.yml` workflow, built by `release.yml` through GoReleaser (`.goreleaser.yaml`), and published as immutable archives, `.deb`/`.rpm` packages, a signed `release-manifest.json` and a moving `v0` tag.
A release manifest is signed as `release.yml@refs/heads/main`, and the policy says so.
A remote lease is charged for the shape, not the tier request.
A remote record may not name a local file that is not durable yet.
A repository has no runner groups, so `groupFor` refuses any named group on a repository target with `ErrNoRunnerGroups` before the service is asked, `ValidateTrustedRunnerGroup` refuses outright, and the Actions service still answers the DEFAULT group there (measured, below), so `EnsureScaleSet`, `Describe` and `DeleteScaleSet` need no repository branch.
A repository target has no runner groups, so nothing on GitHub's side can restrict a pool there: every tier under one is untrusted, refused at load and again at `server.Run` with `trusted`, `runner_group`, `workflows` or `intercept`, which is also why docker cannot serve a repository target.
A repository target: `metadata: read` and `administration: write`, the only permission GitHub offers for registering a repository's runners and a far wider one, disclosed as such by `github-app create --repository`; the two sets are read by exactly one function (`permissionsFor`, asserted structurally) and `PermissionMismatches(scope)` verifies against the set for the target's scope in both directions.
A required network dependency may receive an idempotent start only while already active; any stop refuses.

A retirement's own exclusion acquires and never admits.
A reusable workflow called at the run's own commit is proven for READING only and never writes (#318): a tag named `main` at commit S calling `@refs/heads/main` while the branch is also at S presents exactly what a push to `main` calling a local workflow does, and GitHub records nothing else (no ref type on the run, only `jobWorkflowRef` on the job) that tells them apart.
A revalidating handle re-reads the mark inside every write transaction (`checkReleaseWatermarkIn`, beside the schema re-check), since an older admin handle open across a newer controller's claim would otherwise write.
A reviewer that does not know the App key must never be overwritten cannot tell you that it can be.

A root installer prepares the PACKAGED directory, never the calling account's.
A rotation is an overlap, not a switch, and it is published in an order a lock-free reader can trust.
A row billet cannot read is never sealed over: `AdmissionUnknown` is the fail-closed zero value, and writing a `local-down` seal onto it would turn "could not tell" into a seal the next `up` clears.
A row whose placement facts are unverifiable fails closed, and `Reap` and `Release` deliberately skip those checks so it can always be cleaned up.
A rule about a string that leaves the process is pinned to the boundary it crosses.
A rule that asked one of them loosely would let an outage joined with this host's pools failing to close read as a row a survivor may finish, hiding a fault that host must fix.
A running service is ONE SAMPLE bound to one incarnation: the start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22, a zombie or dead state refusing, because a zombie keeps its start time) before, then the image, the command line, the environment and the process's own view of its `--config` path opened under `/proc/<pid>/root` with root-scoped resolution (`openat2` with `RESOLVE_IN_ROOT` and `RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS`; a plain open of the joined path would resolve an absolute symlink against the inspector's root and open the inspector's own file), then systemd's `MainPID`, `InvocationID`, exec-shaping properties, remapping directives and the structured ExecStart records read again and required equal (a reload that adds a bind mount or moves an argument boundary behind an unchanged rendering discards the sample), then the start time again after that systemd read, so a restart, a pid reuse or a unit edited under the sample is could-not-tell rather than image evidence attributed to a process the other reads saw; on darwin there is no process-bound image and the report says the hash is path evidence.

A takeover (`hold --recover-from OLD --old-driver-stopped`) needs the guard to name OLD exactly, to carry a pointer whose journal reads, and a clean process scan; it rewrites the record through a fresh tmp created exclusively, an existing one examined through an identity descriptor (regular, owned, one link) and removed by name first, keeping the pointer and the executable.
A takeover (`hold --recover-from`) HOLDS THE MARKER TO ITS JOURNAL (`admitRetirementTakeover`): the journal must exist, be the old holder's by owner or chain (`Journal.Validate` with the guard's `TakenOverFrom`), and name the marker's transition, else the record is kept and the refusal names both ids; a marker beside no journal is an abandoned reservation, refused naming `billet server retire --abandon-reservation`; a guard with NO marker is taken over across exactly the tail's crash window (a `done` journal not yet settled, since the tail clears the marker and then writes `settled`) and the takeover RESTORES the marker from the journal's provenance, while no marker beside a settled journal or a journal at any other phase refuses; every takeover keeps the marker and appends the old holder, and a marker beside a pointer is held to the same rule.
A takeover retires the acquirer's window with the holder: the rewritten record carries no `token` and `preparing: false`, because the token authorises the cleanup release by the invocation that acquired the guard and the new holder never did.

An unprovable rollback is cordoned (`ErrCordoned`) with its journal intact.
An unreadable claim deliberately does not abandon: it is no evidence of a successor, and the destroys skipped are for jobs GitHub already concluded.
An unrecognised 404 (no code, a code billet will not repeat to an operator, a body it could not read whole, a root element that is not `<Error>`) stays an error, because could-not-tell never collapses into no.
Ancestor mounts supplying admitted `RequiresMountsFor=` paths, such as a separate `/var` on `/dev/vdb1`, are standard leaves accepted only while active; their own device, blockdev, fstab-passno `systemd-fsck@` service, `local-fs-pre.target`, `local-fs.target`, `systemd-remount-fs.service`, root-mount and tmpfs `swap.target` dependencies are not traversed.
And `ec2:CreateVolume` from a snapshot authorises the snapshot as well, so `BilletCacheCloneSource` grants it on the snapshot ARN conditioned on the owner tag.
And a 404 on a state read is an empty cache only when S3 says `NoSuchKey`: every 404 used to be, so a bucket that did not exist read exactly like a cold cache, every job fetched cold, the cache path fails open by design and `billet check`'s bucket probe reported that the bucket answered.
And a CodeBuild container runs as root, where GitHub's runner prints `Must not run interactively with sudo` and exits zero, so the build succeeded having registered nothing; the buildspec exports `RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1` in the phase that execs the runner, and the test asserts the phase.
And a trailing `[ -s pid ] && printf pid` makes the whole query exit non-zero when there is no pid, which reads as "could not ask" and silently disabled a conclusive verdict in the guest launcher.
And pass commit messages with `-F`: backticks in `git commit -m` are command substitution.
Answers must match that operand and the recorded transition; retained tail receipts are `written` or `current`, server-only tail receipts are `none`, and settled unchanged answers have postconditions without a receipt member.
Any other rbd answer is `could not tell`, keeps the image and exits 1, and a `trash mv` that errored is `move not confirmed` (it may have happened) and exits 1 too.
Anything the model refuses is re-asked as `headroom`, the room the allocator would grant this instant.
Archives are `billet_<version>_<os>_<arch>` (a contract `install.sh` derives from `uname`) carrying `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `billet.example.yaml` and both plists (a Mac has no package).

Base64 of the shared installers and the pinned declaration gzips to 27235 bytes, over by ten kilobytes, because base64 costs 33% before gzip and destroys the redundancy gzip lives on; the same bytes in quoted heredocs with whole-line comments stripped land at 11327.

Because `ssh_access` runs before the host role, the host role's own first-task refusal of a billet-managed runner would fire after a key was installed; each play therefore opens with `include_role: junioryono.billet.host, tasks_from: prepare-exclusion` (whose first task clears per-inclusion permission without a connection, followed by the runner guard's import, and which holds the host under the converge guard before ssh_access runs), tagged `always` on the include and on what it includes so `--tags` cannot skip it, and `fleet-playbook-check` proves the shape and that the refusal leaves no key behind, under `ANSIBLE_HOST_PATTERN_MISMATCH=error` with an empty `macos` group declared, because a targeted group the inventory never declares fails a strict run after the earlier plays converged: the generated inventory and both examples declare all three groups, empty ones as `hosts: {}`.
Because a failed generation removal no longer ends the pass, the generations' part starts no new work once it has held the lock for `evictionLockBudget` (five minutes from the moment the lock is held, index-record removals included, inside `cacheLockWaitLimit`, the longest a writer waits for the lock; the generation in hand still finishes under the command bound), names how many wait for the next pass outside the ten-name cap, and the next pass resumes after the last generation it reached (`evictResume`), so slowly failing generations at the front of the order cannot spend every pass's budget.
Before 2026-09-04 it accepted `refs/heads/release/vX.Y` or `refs/tags/vX.Y.Z` on the belief that release.yml "runs against the tag", so every binary through v0.6.0 refuses every manifest billet has published: `rollout start`, the automatic starter and `host-upgrade --version` all fail on those releases with "the manifest's signature does not satisfy this source's policy", and a fleet on them has to be moved by the Ansible role or the package once.
Before adding a difference, look for GitHub's own fix after the pin (`gh api repos/actions/runner-images/compare/<pin>...main`) and copy its effect.
Before backup handling, an `activating/start` oneshot with a start job may reach the bounded wait, and a failed backup may reach the existing retirement-status reconciliation; only that retirement’s recognised status is cleared.
Before clearing a workspace the build finds every machine by what it holds (machined's `RootDirectory` equal to this rootfs), stops it through the unit machined names, and refuses on a failed listing, an unreadable or empty property, or a machine gone before its root was read.
Before it existed a failed publication held the key for the lease's remaining fifteen minutes and the next writer polled S3 every 100ms with nothing in the log; the wait is now a doubling back-off from 500ms to 30s, never longer than the holder's remaining lease, announced once per lease through `store.WriterHeldError`, which unwraps to `ErrConflict`.
Before it existed a stopped host kept receiving placements for one `staleAfter` window, about four and a half minutes measured.
Before reservation in either mode, `billet_retirement_requested_variant` is selected only from positively observed installed roles; separate assertions refuse an installed node missing from desired inventory and a desired node absent from the installation.
Before reservation, including check mode, `retirement-request.yml` selects `billet_retirement_requested_variant` from the classifier's observed installed roles and separately refuses either direction of node-presence drift; node removal or installation must converge ordinarily with retirement disabled first.
Before submitting a test for an invariant, neuter the production line it names (comment out the `syscall.Flock` in `internal/state/lock_unix.go`, run `TestSecondOpenIsRefused`, watch it fail, restore) and confirm the test goes red.
Before tagging it rewrites the internal composite-action refs and `galaxy.yml` to the release version.
Before that, a tier whose demand kept arriving was never `served`, and its launches counted as progress, so it was never stalled either: on 2026-09-25 a repository's CI backlog held the line for thirty minutes while an organization's tier of the same shape on the same host started nothing, and no bypass warning was logged.
Before this, the cancellation tore down the runner mid-job (GitHub refused the removal), recorded `canceled` on its lease so the real result was later refused as a contradiction, and acknowledged its completion source; that journal holds 29, 82 and 59 mid-job removal refusals on 2026-09-17, 21 and 22 (#189).
Before v0.9.1 each half waited for the other and every self-upgrade hung at the probe with the services stopped.

Beside no journal, `--requested` selects `new-request` for an eligible installed controller whether or not it keeps a node; `route_why` names the variant the request will carry.

Details that each cost a debugging session to learn:
Determinism comes from delivering one event at a time to quiescence, where quiescence means every listener is parked on an empty queue with its advertisement unchanged since its last poll, because the listener hands surplus escrow back only after a poll carrying the smaller number has returned.
Diagnostics that pipe into `head` fail a passing gate.

Docker `--filter name=` is a substring match.
Docker gets it in an env file, firecracker in MMDS placed before `InstanceStart`, tart on stdin through `tart exec -i` to the guest agent's socket (never the clone, never SSH), EC2 in single-use instance user data with `HttpTokens=required` and `HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1` so a container inside the job cannot reach the metadata service, and CodeBuild in an SSM SecureString resolved by the service into `ACTIONS_RUNNER_INPUT_JITCONFIG`, so only the parameter's name is ever rendered.
Docker image stores are scoped by deployment, site and architecture, so a private image pulled by one trusted job is readable by every later job in that boundary.
